summaries.example: Imagine that you are testing the idea “all the apples in this basket are red.” Finding one red apple fits the idea and gives it some support. Finding a green apple counts against it. But finding a red apple does not prove that every apple is red, because there may be another apple you have not checked.
summaries.summary: Confirmation is about how evidence affects our confidence in an idea. A doctor, scientist, or student may use observations to support a hypothesis, but evidence does not always guarantee the conclusion. Several competing theories try to explain this kind of reasoning. Hempel’s theory focuses on confirming examples of general rules. Hypothetico-deductivism asks whether a hypothesis, together with background assumptions, would lead us to expect the evidence. Bayesian theories use probabilities to measure how evidence changes belief. The entry also studies puzzles, such as why a green apple might seem to support the claim that all ravens are black, and why strange rules can fit the same evidence. These puzzles show that good reasoning needs more than simply matching an observation to a rule.
key_ideas: Evidence can support a hypothesis without proving it completely.
A single observation may fit more than one possible explanation.
Hempel’s approach says that an example of a general rule can support that rule, but it faces puzzles.
Other approaches ask whether a hypothesis predicts the evidence, explains it, or makes the evidence more likely.
Bayesian approaches use probabilities to describe how evidence changes confidence in a hypothesis.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use evidence when making predictions, learning, diagnosing problems, and deciding which explanation to trust. Understanding confirmation helps us see why a conclusion can be reasonable without being certain. It also reminds us to ask whether the evidence is relevant, whether other explanations are possible, and whether a surprising result really tests an idea.

important_terms.definition: Information or an observation that gives us a reason to believe, doubt, or compare ideas.
An idea or claim that evidence may support or weaken.
Support for a hypothesis from evidence. Confirmation can make an idea more believable without making it certain.
Reasoning that goes beyond what is strictly proved by the facts already known. It can be useful but can also be mistaken.

questions_to_think_about: Does finding one red apple really tell you that every apple is red?
Would finding an apple that is not red change your mind? How much?
Can the same piece of evidence support two different explanations?
Why might a surprising observation be more useful than an expected one?

summaries.example: Suppose a researcher studies whether a new treatment works. The hypothesis h says that the treatment improves patients’ health, while background assumptions k include how patients were selected and how improvement is measured. Evidence e is that treated patients improve. On a hypothetico-deductive view, e supports h if h together with k entails e, while k alone does not. A Bayesian relevance view instead asks whether P(h | e and k) is greater than P(h | k). The first framework emphasizes a prediction; the second emphasizes a change in probability. Neither automatically settles how strong the support is.
summaries.summary:
The entry examines confirmation as the non-deductive relation between evidence and hypotheses. Since evidence rarely entails a general theory, confirmation theory seeks more nuanced accounts of evidential support. Hempel’s instance-based theory formalizes the thought that an observed F that is also G supports the universal claim that all Fs are Gs. Yet the ravens paradox suggests that a non-black non-raven can support “all ravens are black,” while the blite construction shows that the same observation can support bizarre, time-dependent predicates. Hempel’s account also struggles with scientific cases in which observations and theories use different vocabularies, requiring auxiliary assumptions.

Hypothetico-deductivism reverses the direction of deduction: a hypothesis is supported when, together with auxiliaries, it entails evidence that the auxiliaries alone do not entail. This captures prediction and can avoid some Hempelian consequences, but naïve HD fails to preserve several plausible principles, including a general link from confirming a universal law to confirming a prediction about a further case. It also faces underdetermination: suitable auxiliaries can make almost any consistent hypothesis entail an observation. Proposed repairs appeal to novel prediction, use-novelty, elimination of alternatives, simplicity, or explanation; the entry presents these as important options rather than a settled solution.

Bayesian theories represent belief with probabilities. One major distinction is between firmness, where evidence leaves a hypothesis more probable than not, and relevance, where evidence raises its probability relative to its prior value. Relevance measures can represent degrees of support and distinguish evidence that is merely compatible with a hypothesisمرan
key_ideas: Hume’s challenge shows why reasoning from observed cases to general laws is fallible: logically compatible alternatives may remain.

Hempelian confirmation treats suitable instances of a universal hypothesis as confirming it, but the ravens and blite puzzles make this approach too permissive in some cases and too restrictive in others.

Hypothetico-deductivism treats confirmation as a reversed use of deduction: a hypothesis plus auxiliaries predicts evidence. It avoids some ravens problems but faces irrelevant-conjunction and underdetermination difficulties.

The Duhemian challenge emphasizes that scientific theories usually need auxiliary assumptions to connect unobservable structures with observations. Formal logic alone may then allow many competing confirmations.
Bayesian approaches distinguish firmness, a high posterior probability, from relevance, an increase from prior to posterior probability. These are not the same.

Bayesian measures can compare degrees of support and illuminate issues involving surprising evidence, variety of evidence, old evidence, and the ravens paradox, although disputes about probabilities and measures remain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Confirmation theory matters because scientific reasoning, diagnosis, prediction, and everyday learning all depend on judging how much evidence supports a claim. The competing approaches reveal different standards: matching instances, deriving predictions, increasing probability, ruling out alternatives, simplicity, and explanatory power. Studying their successes and problems helps clarify why evidence can be genuinely useful while still leaving room for error and disagreement.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of how evidence supports, weakens, or leaves unchanged a hypothesis.
A relation in which evidence raises the credibility or evidential standing of a hypothesis, without normally entailing it.
Logical consequence: if premises are true, an entailed conclusion must be true. Confirmation theories debate how this deductive relation should matter to non-deductive support.
The idea that evidence confirms a hypothesis when the hypothesis, with auxiliary assumptions, entails the evidence, but the auxiliaries alone do not.
Additional assumptions needed to connect a hypothesis with an observation, such as measurement conditions or laws governing an experiment.
The problem that available evidence may fit several incompatible hypotheses, especially when auxiliary assumptions can be adjusted.
A family of approaches representing degrees of belief with probabilities and studying how evidence changes those degrees.
Confirmation understood as an increase in a hypothesis’s probability after evidence, rather than merely a high final probability.

questions_to_think_about: Should a theory receive support from evidence that it was designed to fit, or only from evidence that it predicted independently?
How should a confirmation theory handle auxiliary assumptions without allowing them to be chosen ad hoc?
Is a hypothesis confirmed when its probability becomes high, or whenever its probability increases?
Why does observing a non-raven seem less informative about ravens than observing a black raven?
Can a theory explain evidence well while still receiving little confirmation from it?

summaries.example: A class wants to test the claim “all the plants in our school garden need the same amount of water.” One dry plant might support the claim if it belongs to the group being studied, but it does not prove the claim. The class also needs background information: Was the plant in sunlight? Was its soil similar? A hypothetico-deductive thinker asks whether the claim plus these background assumptions would predict the dry plant. A Bayesian thinker asks whether seeing the dry plant makes the claim more or less probable than it was before.
summaries.summary:
Confirmation theory asks how evidence changes the credibility of hypotheses. This question matters because reasoning in science and everyday life is usually not deductive proof: several explanations may fit the same observations, and even accurate evidence can lead to a wrong conclusion. Hempel’s theory develops the idea that observing an object with both properties F and G supports the general claim that all F-objects are G. It also treats an F-object lacking G as evidence against that claim. However, the ravens paradox shows a problem: because “all ravens are black” is logically equivalent to “all non-black things are non-ravens,” observing a green apple can seem to support the raven claim. The blite example creates another puzzle by defining an artificial property that changes with when an object is examined.

Hypothetico-deductive reasoning takes a different route. A hypothesis is supported when it, combined with suitable auxiliary assumptions, entails an observation that the auxiliaries alone do not entail. This highlights prediction and testing, but it can make confirmation too easy if auxiliaries are adjusted whenever needed. This is connected with underdetermination, the idea that evidence may not select one theory uniquely. Philosophers have proposed strengthening HD with requirements such as novel prediction, use-novelty, successful elimination of alternatives, simplicity, or explanation. Each proposal captures something important but also faces questions.

Bayesian approaches use probabilities. A firmness view asks how probable a hypothesis is after the evidence, while a relevance view asks whether its probability increased because of the evidence. key_ideas: Evidence can support a claim without making it certain; mistakes can remain possible even when the evidence is true and extensive.
Hempel’s theory says that an observed example of a general rule confirms that rule, while an exception disconfirms it.
The ravens paradox challenges the idea that every logically equivalent supporting example is equally informative.
Hypothetico-deductive reasoning focuses on what a hypothesis predicts with the help of background assumptions.
Naïve hypothetico-deductivism can make support too easy because different auxiliary assumptions may connect almost any consistent hypothesis to the evidence.
Bayesian theories distinguish a hypothesis becoming more probable from a hypothesis ending up highly probable. They also allow comparisons of stronger and weaker support.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often hear that evidence “proves” or “supports” something, but those words can hide important differences. Confirmation theory gives us tools for asking how strong the support is, whether background assumptions are doing too much work, and whether another hypothesis explains the same facts. These questions are central to science, medicine, learning, and careful decision-making.

important_terms.definition: A fact, observation, or statement used to evaluate a claim.
A claim proposed as an explanation or general rule and tested against evidence.
The study of when and how evidence supports or weakens hypotheses.
Reasoning in which a general claim, together with background assumptions, is used to derive an observation that can test the claim.
Background claims needed to connect a theory to a test, such as assumptions about instruments, samples, or conditions.
A situation in which the same evidence is compatible with more than one hypothesis.
An approach that uses probability to represent confidence and examines how evidence changes it.
A puzzle about whether observing something that is neither black nor a raven supports the claim that all ravens are black.

questions_to_think_about: If two pieces of evidence are logically related, must they be equally helpful?
When does a background assumption help a test, and when does it make the test unfair?
Why might a surprising prediction provide stronger support than an obvious one?
Can evidence make a claim more likely even if the claim is still unlikely overall?
What should count as a good explanation besides simply fitting the facts?
